title: The ladder of names
hookLine: Dionysius the Areopagite: God beyond names, beyond being

cards: At the end of a chapter in Acts, after a speech, comes a short list of the people who stayed behind: "Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them."
That's all the Bible tells us about him. A name in a list.
The speech had started from an altar with no god's name on it, and Paul read its inscription aloud: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you."
Later, writings appeared under his name that go straight back to that altar, asking whether not knowing God's name could be where wisdom starts.

teach.b: The texts claim the name of that listener from Acts.

Modern scholars generally read them as written much later by an unknown author, and call him Pseudo-Dionysius; Orthodox tradition still honors them under the name Dionysius. What they teach is a ladder that runs two ways.
Going down, you name God. Scripture gives plenty of names: good, light, life, wisdom, love. In The Divine Names, Dionysius treats them one by one, and says each is true.
God really is good. God really is light.

teach.h: UP THE LADDER: TAKE THE NAMES OFF.
teach.b: Then the climb back up runs the other way: you take the names off, starting from the lowest. God is not a rock, not a fire, not a king the way kings are kings. Keep climbing, and even the high names come off.
God is not good the way we know good, not even being the way things are. Not because God is less, but because God is beyond.
Dionysius says God is both the one with many names and the nameless one. At the top there's no more talking.

teach.h: THE THICK DARKNESS WHERE GOD WAS.
teach.b: He points to Moses on the mountain: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." A darkness, Dionysius says, that's actually too much light.
This way of speaking is called apophatic: speaking of God by saying what God is not. Eastern Orthodox theology makes much of it, and Western mystics drew on it too.
It gave Christians a humility in words: every name is true, and every name falls short.

how: Eastern Orthodox Christians in particular speak of the apophatic way, approaching God by saying what God is not; Christians of different churches practice wordless prayer in the same spirit.

games.q: what does “the ladder of names” mean?
o: the family line from Adam to Jesus in the Gospels
a list of God's names, ranked from least to most holy
naming God, then taking the names off, step by step

games.q: the ladder of names — tap the pairs.
p: an altar to the unknown God
drew near unto the thick darkness

s: Dionysius says the names of God in scripture are false
he says each is true, and each falls short: God has many names and is nameless.
the Bible tells us only a little about Dionysius the Areopagite
Acts names him as one who believed after Paul spoke in Athens, and says no more.
saying what God is not means God is less
for Dionysius it means God is beyond: a darkness that's too much light.

games.q: you're Paul in Athens. you find an altar inscribed to an unknown god. what do you do?
o: tell the Athenians the altar is meaningless.
start from the altar: the God you don't know, I'll declare to you.
games.why: Paul starts right there: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you." Dionysius was among those who stayed.

practice: If you pray, say one name you use for God, Father, Lord, light, love, slowly, inside; if you don't, choose a word for whatever is biggest to you.
Then let even that word go quiet, and stay in the space it pointed toward without filling it. When a new word rushes in, notice it, and set it down.

wordCard.voice: The ladder of names. Name God from scripture going down; take the names off going up, until there's only the thick darkness where God was.

orig.note: Greek: denial, saying no. apophatic speech speaks of God by saying what God is not.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond every name. Even the very best name points past itself. Until tomorrow.
